opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that AI workloads are fundamentally different from the workloads the existing stack was built for. If you look at the last couple of decades, most of the infrastructure, the databases, the big data systems like Hadoop and Spark, even the cloud itself, was designed around CPUs and largely structured data. You have tables, you run SQL queries, you do ETL, and the computation is fairly homogeneous.

AI changes almost every one of these assumptions. First, the hardware is heterogeneous. You have GPUs, TPUs, other accelerators, and they're scarce and very expensive. So utilization matters enormously, and you need to schedule across CPUs and GPUs in the same application. A typical pipeline might do data preprocessing on CPUs, then training or inference on GPUs, then post-processing again on CPUs. Existing systems weren't built to handle that mix efficiently.

Second, the data is different. More and more of it is unstructured: images, video, audio, text documents. Processing this data is much more compute-intensive than processing rows in a table. And it's not just about storing and querying it; you're running models over it.

Third, the scale. Training these large models requires thousands of accelerators working together, and even serving them is a distributed systems problem now. A single model may not fit on one GPU. So you need to deal with distribution, fault tolerance, and scheduling at a level that most developers never had to think about before.

And finally, the applications themselves are changing. With LLMs, you're building what we call compound AI systems, where you have multiple models calling each other, retrieval, tools, agents. These applications are non-deterministic. The same input can produce different outputs, which breaks a lot of our assumptions about testing, debugging, and reliability.

So when you put all of this together, it's not enough to patch the existing stack. You need to rethink things from the ground up: how you schedule resources, how you process data, how you serve models, how you evaluate and debug applications. That's really what motivated a lot of our work, starting with Ray. We saw that developers needed a simple way to scale these heterogeneous, distributed AI workloads without becoming distributed systems experts themselves.

r001.rationale: It says large models may not fit on one GPU and require thousands of accelerators, but does not state that AI demands are growing faster than a single compute node’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes heterogeneous hardware and the need to schedule across CPUs and GPUs, but does not explain that accelerators are being introduced to bridge a demand–capability gap.

r003.rationale: It says developers need a simple way to scale heterogeneous, distributed AI workloads without becoming distributed systems experts, conveying that the stack should hide that complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that the workload has changed in a fundamental way, and historically every time the workload changes this much, the stack changes with it. We saw this with big data. You had Hadoop, then Spark, and an entire ecosystem grew up around the fact that data was now too big for one machine and you needed distributed processing. AI is a bigger shift than that, because it changes not just the scale but the nature of what the software is doing.

Think about what a traditional application looks like. It's deterministic. You write code, you give it an input, you get a predictable output, and if it's wrong you can debug it line by line. AI applications are not like that. At the center you have a model, which is a statistical object. The same input can produce different outputs. You can't step through it with a debugger. And increasingly it's not just one model call, it's a chain of calls, with tools, with retrieval, with agents that take actions and loop back. So the unit of computation is different, the failure modes are different, and the performance characteristics are totally different.

Then there's the hardware side. For decades we built software on the assumption that CPUs are the workhorse and they get faster every year. Now the compute that matters is GPUs and accelerators, which are expensive, scarce, and quite hard to use efficiently. If you look at how most people serve or train models, the utilization of that hardware is embarrassingly low. So you need new schedulers, new serving systems, new ways to manage memory. That's a lot of what motivated things like Ray, and later vLLM. The old assumptions about resource management just don't hold.

And the third piece is the developer. The people building these applications often aren't systems people. They're writing Python, they're iterating quickly, they want to go from a laptop to a cluster without rewriting everything. So the abstractions need to hide the distributed complexity while still giving you performance. That tension, simplicity for the developer and efficiency on very expensive hardware, is really the core problem, and I don't think the existing stack was designed with either of those constraints in mind. So it's not that everything gets thrown away, but a surprising fraction of it, from the compute layer to how you evaluate and monitor these systems, has to be reconsidered.

r001.rationale: The response says AI changes the workload and that GPUs and accelerators are expensive and scarce, but it does not state that AI demands outgrow a single node’s capabilities even with accelerators.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift from CPU assumptions to GPUs and accelerators, but does not explain that adding accelerators to meet application demands increases infrastructure heterogeneity.

r003.rationale: It says abstractions should hide distributed complexity from developers, but does not state that they should also hide the complexity of heterogeneous infrastructure.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental reason is that AI changes the workload, and when the workload changes significantly, the software stack has to change with it. Traditionally, you write down the logic of an application explicitly. With AI, much of that behavior comes from a model trained on data. So now you have to manage not only code, but also data, models, training, and inference—and understand how changes in any of these affect the application.

The computation is also different. You have very intensive workloads running on accelerators, often distributed across many machines. Moving data, scheduling computation, and managing memory become critical to both performance and cost. The abstractions we built for traditional applications don’t always make those things easy.

And at the application level, the output is not necessarily predictable. That changes how you test, debug, and monitor the system. It’s not enough to ask whether the software executed correctly; you also have to ask whether the answer was useful or accurate.

So it’s not that every existing component becomes obsolete. But the requirements change across enough layers that we need to rethink the stack as a whole.

r001.rationale: The response describes intensive accelerator workloads across many machines, but does not state that AI demands outgrow a single compute node even with accelerators.

r002.rationale: It mentions accelerators and distributed machines, but does not explain that using accelerators to bridge a demand-capability gap increases infrastructure heterogeneity.

r003.rationale: It says traditional abstractions may not make infrastructure tasks easy, but does not state that the stack must hide distributed, heterogeneous infrastructure complexity from application developers.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, AI changes some of the basic assumptions that our software stack was built around. Traditionally, you write down the logic of an application, and the software executes that logic. With AI, a lot of the behavior comes from a model and from the data you give it. So now you have to manage not only code, but also data, models, and how they interact.

And the workloads are different. Training is computationally intensive, but serving models also introduces challenges: how do you get low latency, how do you use accelerators efficiently, how do you control cost? Then, at the application level, the output is probabilistic. Testing whether an application works is no longer just checking that you get one expected answer.

So I don’t mean that we should throw away everything we’ve built. But we need to revisit the abstractions across the stack, from the infrastructure to the tools developers use, to make these applications easier to build and operate reliably.

r001.rationale: The response mentions computationally intensive training and efficient accelerator use, but does not say AI demands exceed what a single node can provide, even with accelerators.

r002.rationale: It mentions accelerators and infrastructure, but does not explain that adding accelerators increases infrastructure heterogeneity.

r003.rationale: It calls for revisiting abstractions across the stack to make applications easier to build and operate, but does not state that the stack should hide the complexity of distributed, heterogeneous infrastructure from developers.
